Why Gross Changes Are Absent at 8 Hours

Myocardial infarction (MI) is the necrosis of cardiac myocytes due to ischaemia. The temporal evolution of morphological changes in MI is well-defined, and grossly visible changes typically do not appear until 12–24 hours after the onset of ischaemia. At 8 hours, the infarcted tissue is still in the early phase of coagulative necrosis — cell architecture is preserved (ghost outlines of myocytes) but the tissue has not yet accumulated enough oedema, neutrophil infiltrate, or haemorrhage to become visibly discoloured. Therefore, the gross appearance of the myocardium remains essentially normal — no pallor, no hyperaemic border, no yellow softening.

The earliest gross changes — pallor of the subendocardial region and a hyperaemic border — appear around 12 hours; the classic yellow, soft, hyperaemic-ringed infarct becomes evident only after ~24 hours. Thus an 8-hour-old infarct is morphologically silent to the naked eye.

Earliest Microscopic Changes (Expected at 8 Hours)

  • Wavy fibres — the earliest change (within 1–2 hours). Ischaemic myocytes lose contractility but adjacent viable fibres continue contracting, pulling the necrotic fibres into a wavy configuration.
  • Coagulative necrosis — starts at ~4–6 hours; myocyte nuclei become pyknotic, then disappear (karyorrhexis), but the cell outline is preserved.
  • Hyper-eosinophilia (by 6–8 hours) — cytoplasm of necrotic myocytes stains deeper pink with eosin due to protein denaturation & loss of cytoplasmic glycogen.
  • Neutrophil margination & early infiltration — starts at the periphery of the infarct by ~6–8 hours and peaks at 24 hours.
  • Interstitial oedema & focal haemorrhage.
  • Contraction band necrosis — hypercontracted sarcomeres with dense eosinophilic transverse bands; seen when perfusion is restored (reperfusion injury) or in non-occlusive infarcts.

Chronological Summary

TimeGrossMicroscopic
0–4 hNormalNo change / wavy fibres
4–12 hNormal or slight pallorCoagulative necrosis, hyper-eosinophilia, early neutrophils
12–24 hPale / hyperaemic rimNeutrophil infiltrate peaks
1–3 dYellow, soft, hyperaemic rimNeutrophil infiltration, necrosis well developed
3–7 dYellow, soft, hyperaemic rimMacrophages, granulation tissue at margins

Clinical Pearl

The absence of gross changes within the first 12 hours is a favourite viva question because it underscores a key clinicopathological principle: function is lost before morphology appears. A patient can die of cardiogenic shock from an MI that is invisible to the naked eye at autopsy. To confirm an early infarct, use histochemistry (dehydrogenase stain — nitro-BT fails to stain infarcted myocardium blue because enzymes are lost) or immunohistochemistry for cardiac troponin depletion / myoglobin loss in the first 4–6 hours — long before routine H&E reveals changes.

Introduction

The sputum eosinophilia in this patient with recurrent wheeze and bronchodilator response is the hallmark of bronchial asthma, a chronic inflammatory airway disease characterised by reversible airflow obstruction, airway hyper-responsiveness (AHR), and remodelling. Eosinophils are not merely a marker — they are central effectors of airway damage.

Role of Eosinophils — Mechanism

  1. Recruitment & activation — inhaled allergens activate sensitised Th2 cells → release IL-5, IL-4, IL-13. IL-5 drives eosinopoiesis in bone marrow, release into circulation, and survival within tissue. Eotaxin (CCL11) & RANTES (CCL5) recruit eosinophils into the bronchial mucosa via CCR3; VCAM-1 on endothelium mediates adhesion via VLA-4.
  2. Activation & degranulation — eosinophils activated by IL-5, IgE immune complexes, leukotrienes, and platelet-activating factor release four categories of cytotoxic granule proteins:
    • Major basic protein (MBP) — directly damages airway epithelium, causes ciliary dysfunction and shedding, triggers histamine release from mast cells.
    • Eosinophil cationic protein (ECP) — creates cytotoxic pores in epithelial cells; correlates with asthma severity.
    • Eosinophil peroxidase (EPO) — generates reactive oxygen species & hypohalous acids → oxidative tissue injury.
    • Eosinophil-derived neurotoxin (EDN / RNase 2) — damages airway nerves, promotes neurogenic inflammation.
  3. Lipid mediator release — eosinophils generate leukotriene C4, D4, E4 (slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis) → potent bronchoconstrictors (1000× histamine), mucus hypersecretion, increased vascular permeability; platelet-activating factor (PAF) sustains AHR.
  4. Cytine release — IL-5 (autocrine survival), IL-13 (goblet cell hyperplasia & mucus), TGF-β (drives airway remodelling — sub-basement membrane fibrosis, smooth muscle hyperplasia).
  5. Epithelial damage & airway remodelling — MBP & ECP strip the ciliated epithelium, exposing sensory nerve endings (C-fibres) → heightened cough reflex & AHR. Chronic eosinophilia drives subepithelial fibrosis, smooth muscle hypertrophy, goblet cell metaplasia — features of fixed obstruction.

Consequences

  • Bronchoconstriction (immediate — LTs, histamine; late — eosinophil-mediated).
  • Mucus plugging of bronchi (Charcot-Leyden crystals — bipyramidal crystals from eosinophil membrane phospholipase; Curschmann spirals — mucus casts).
  • Thickened basement membrane; airway remodelling.
  • Cor pulmonale in chronic severe asthma.

Clinical Pearl

Sputum eosinophilia is so reliable in asthma that the term eosinophilic asthma defines a treatable phenotype (~50–60% of asthmatics). This is the rationale for anti-IL-5 biologics (mepolizumab, reslizumab, benralizumab) in severe eosinophilic asthma — they reduce exacerbations and steroid dependence by depleting eosinophils. Conversely, neutrophilic asthma (Th17-driven) responds poorly to steroids and requires different targeting, illustrating why sputum cell counts guide phenotype-directed therapy.

Introduction

Differentiating a benign soft tissue tumour from a malignant soft tissue sarcoma is clinically critical because sarcomas metastasise haematogenously and require wide excision. While definitive diagnosis needs histopathology, the distinction rests on a combination of clinical, radiological, and histological features.

Histological Criteria (FNCLCC / NCI grading)

Feature Benign Malignant (Sarcoma)
SizeUsually <5 cmOften >5 cm
GrowthSlow, well-circumscribed, encapsulated, pushing marginsRapid, infiltrative, irregular margins
CellularityLow; resembles parent tissueHypercellular; loss of normal architecture
PleomorphismMinimal; uniform cellsMarked — variation in size/shape, nuclear hyperchromasia
NucleusSmall, regular, fine chromatinEnlarged, coarse chromatin, prominent nucleoli
MitosesRare, normalIncreased (≥5/10 HPF), atypical forms (tripolar, ring)
NecrosisAbsentPresent (geographic, map-like)
InvasionNone; expansileInfiltrates surrounding tissue, vessels, nerves
MetastasisAbsentHaematogenous (lung most common); lymphatic in synovial, epithelioid, clear cell, angiosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma
RecurrenceRare after complete excisionHigh; depends on grade & margin

Clinical & Radiological Clues

  • Clinical red flags — size >5 cm, deep to fascia, rapid growth, pain, recurrence after excision. Mnemonic: GPS — Growing, Painful, Size >5 cm.
  • MRI — deep, heterogeneous, T2 hyperintense mass with infiltrative margins and necrosis suggests malignancy. MR features alone cannot exclude sarcoma — biopsy is mandatory.
  • Biopsy — Tru-cut core needle biopsy preferred; placed along the line of future incision so the tract is excised at definitive surgery.

Clinical Pearl

The single most reliable histological discriminator is mitotic activity — especially atypical mitoses, which are essentially pathognomonic of malignancy. However, exceptions exist: atypical lipomatous tumour / well-differentiated liposarcoma may show minimal atypia yet still recur; conversely nodular fasciitis is mitotically active but benign (self-limiting). Diagnosis always requires clinicopathological correlation and increasingly molecular profiling (e.g., MDM2 amplification in WD liposarcoma; SS18-SSX fusion in synovial sarcoma). All suspected sarcomas should be referred to a specialist sarcoma centre before excision — unplanned resection is the most common cause of inadequate margins.

Most Likely Diagnosis

The clinical picture is classic for Crohn's disease (regional enteritis) — a chronic relapsing-remitting granulomatous inflammatory bowel disease of unknown aetiology.

Justification — Three Pathological Features

  1. Discontinuous (skip-lesion) involvement of the terminal ileum — segmental disease with normal intervening mucosa is the cardinal distinguishing feature from ulcerative colitis, which is continuous from the rectum. Terminal ileal localisation is the most common site of Crohn's disease (~30–40% ileocaecal).
  2. Transmural inflammation — biopsy / resection reveals inflammatory infiltrate extending through all layers (mucosa → serosa), producing the thickened rigid bowel wall, fat wrapping, and the propensity for fistulae (entero-enteric, enterocutaneous, perianal) — exactly as in this patient's perianal fistulae. UC, by contrast, is confined to mucosa/submucosa.
  3. Non-caseating granulomas (~30–50% of cases) — present in any layer of the bowel wall and even in regional lymph nodes. Their presence is highly suggestive of Crohn's, though absence does not exclude the diagnosis.

Supporting Clinical & Pathological Clues

  • Chronic diarrhoea (frequently non-bloody, unlike UC), abdominal pain, weight loss — classic triad.
  • Perianal fistulae — occur in ~20–30% of Crohn's patients; sentinel tag, fissure, or abscess may precede intestinal symptoms by years.
  • Cobblestone mucosa & aphthous ulcers (early lesion overlying lymphoid follicles) on endoscopy.
  • Linear / serpiginous deep ulcers → fissures.
  • Strictures ("string sign" on barium) — lead to obstruction, cramping abdominal pain.
  • Fat wrapping (creeping fat) on the serosal aspect.
  • Serositis → adhesions, abscesses.

Clinical Pearl

Perianal fistulising Crohn's disease is a distinct phenotype that often predicts a more aggressive disease course. The ASCA (anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibody) is positive in ~50–70% of Crohn's patients and helps differentiate from UC (p-ANCA positive). Management has been revolutionised by anti-TNF biologics (infliximab, adalimumab) — these close fistulae and reduce granulomatous inflammation. Remember: smoking worsens Crohn's but protects UC — a paradox useful in viva discussions.
q0_1_3_4:
Definition

Endometriosis is the presence of functional endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterine cavity — most commonly in the pelvis. It affects ~10% of reproductive-age women and is a leading cause of chronic pelvic pain and infertility.

Pathogenesis — Multiple Theories (NOT mutually exclusive)

  1. Retrograde menstruation theory (Sampson, 1927) — the most widely accepted. Menstrual debris flows retrograde through fallopian tubes into the peritoneal cavity during menstruation, implants on peritoneal/ovarian surfaces. Supports ovarian & pelvic predominance; explains why endometriosis is rare before menarche and after menopause.
  2. Celomic metaplasia theory (Meyer) — pelvic peritoneum (celomic epithelium) undergoes metaplasia into endometrial-type tissue under hormonal influence. Explains endometriosis in women with amenorrhoea / Müllerian agenesis, and in rare male cases (prostatic stromal tissue).
  3. Induction theory — menstrual debris or other stimuli induce undifferentiated celomic mesenchyme to form endometriotic tissue.
  4. Lymphovascular / haematogenous dissemination (Halban) — explains rare distant sites: lung, brain, ureters, surgical scars (laparotomy, episiotomy).
  5. Stem cell theory — bone marrow-derived stem cells may differentiate into endometriotic tissue.

Permissive factors — genetic predisposition (sister 6× risk), immune dysfunction (impaired clearance of refluxed endometrial cells by NK cells & macrophages), oestrogen dependence (progesterone resistance), low body mass index, prolonged menstrual exposure (nulliparity, short cycles, menorrhagia), Müllerian anomalies with outflow obstruction. SAMPS mnemonic: Sampson + Altered immunity + Metaplasia + Peritoneal + Stem cells.

Morphology

  • Gross — multiple, small (1 mm – 2 cm) black/brown "powder-burn" / "gunpowder" lesions on peritoneum; red flame-like implants (early, vascular); yellow-brown deposits; endometrioma ("chocolate cyst") — ovarian cyst filled with old blood & haemosiderin; dense adhesions, "frozen pelvis" in advanced disease.
  • Microscopy — two of three: endometrial glands, endometrial stroma, & haemosiderin-laden macrophages. Glands show cyclic response to ovarian hormones (menstruate → bleed → inflammation → fibrosis → adhesions).

Two Common Sites

  1. Ovaries (most common, ~60–80%) — usually bilateral; surface implants or endometriomas ("chocolate cysts") that rupture causing acute pelvic pain & adhesions.
  2. Peritoneum — cul-de-sac of Douglas, broad ligament, uterosacral ligaments, fallopian tubes — pain on defecation / dyspareunia; nodularity of uterosacral ligaments on vaginal exam.

Other sites: rectovaginal septum, sigmoid colon (cyclical rectal bleeding), bladder (cyclical haematuria), caesarean/laparotomy scars (cyclical pain & swelling), umbilicus, lung (cyclical haemoptysis — catamenial), brain.

Clinical Pearl

The classic triad — dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia, dyschezia — with infertility should always raise suspicion of endometriosis. Laparoscopy with biopsy remains the gold standard for diagnosis; imaging (transvaginal ultrasound endometrioma; MRI for deep infiltrating disease) is supportive. Importantly, severity of pain does not correlate with extent of disease — a few tiny peritoneal implants can cause severe pain while large endometriomas may be asymptomatic. Medical suppression of ovarian cyclicity (combined OCPs, progestins, GnRH analogues) and surgical ablation/excision are complementary; definitive treatment is total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy in women completed family.

Identification

The ovarian tumour containing hair, teeth and sebaceous material is the classic gross appearance of a mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst) — the most common ovarian germ cell tumour, accounting for ~25–40% of all ovarian tumours, typically in women aged 20–40 years.

Pathological Basis of the Gross Findings

The hair, teeth, and sebaceous material are differentiated somatic tissues arising from all three embryonic germ cell layers. The pathological basis is monodermal / pluripotent differentiation of a primordial germ cell:

  • Hair & sebaceous material — ectodermal differentiation: skin, hair follicles, sebaceous and sweat glands lining the cyst wall. Sebum + desquamated keratin form the yellow, greasy contents. Hair represents mature pilar differentiation.
  • Teeth — mesodermal (dentin/pulp) + ectodermal (enamel from ameloblasts) differentiation; ~30% of dermoids contain one or more teeth, usually at the Rokitansky protuberance (a nipple-like projection from the cyst wall into the lumen where tissue elements are most concentrated).
  • Other elements — cartilage, bone, muscle, thyroid tissue (struma ovarii — 5–15% contain thyroid), neural tissue, bronchial & GI epithelium.

Why Is It Classified as a Germ Cell Tumour?

  1. Cell of origin — primordial germ cells of the ovary. These are totipotent cells that migrate from the yolk sac endoderm to the gonadal ridge during embryogenesis. Their pluripotency allows differentiation into any somatic cell type — explaining the bizarre mix of adult tissues.
  2. Parthenogenetic origin — cytogenetic studies show the tumour arises from a single germ cell after the first meiotic division (XX karyotype, homozygous at many loci). This is supported by isoenzyme studies (G6PD) showing monoclonal origin from one X chromosome.
  3. WHO classification — teratomas are grouped under germ cell tumours alongside dysgerminoma, yolk sac tumour, choriocarcinoma, embryonal carcinoma — because they all arise from germ cells, despite mature teratomas showing fully differentiated somatic tissues.

Morphology

  • Gross — unilocular cyst, 5–10 cm, smooth surface; filled with thick yellow sebum & hair; mural nodule (Rokitansky protuberance) harbouring teeth/bone/cartilage; usually unilateral (bilateral in 10–15%).
  • Microscopy — cyst wall lined by epidermis with granulosa layer; hair follicles, sebaceous & sweat glands in dermis; chunks of adipose tissue, cartilage, neural tissue; Rokitansky protuberance shows diverse tissues including GI/respiratory epithelium, thyroid.

Variants & Complications

  • Immature teratoma — contains immature neuroepithelial elements; malignant, affects younger patients, grows rapidly.
  • Monodermal teratomas — struma ovarii (predominantly thyroid tissue), carcinoid tumour, strumal carcinoid.
  • Somatic malignant transformation — squamous cell carcinoma (most common), melanoma, sarcoma — in ~1–2% of dermoids, usually in older women.
  • Torsion (acute abdomen), rupture (granulomatous peritonitis), infection.

Clinical Pearl

The presence of fat, hair, and calcification (teeth) on pelvic ultrasound or CT is virtually diagnostic of a dermoid cyst — ultrasound shows a highly echogenic mass with dense acoustic shadowing (the "tip of the iceberg" sign) and the "dermoid mesh" sign (hair in fluid). Because 10–15% are bilateral, always examine both ovaries at surgery. Despite being benign, surgical excision (cystectomy with ovarian preservation) is recommended to prevent torsion, rupture, and the small risk of malignant transformation. Recurrence rate after cystectomy is ~3–4% over 5 years.

Introduction

Anemia of chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a normocytic normochromic anemia that typically develops when eGFR falls below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² and becomes nearly universal at eGFR <30 (stage 4–5 CKD). It is multifactorial, with erythropoietin deficiency the dominant mechanism.

Mechanisms

  1. Reduced erythropoietin (EPO) production — the central mechanism
    • EPO is produced by peritubular interstitial fibroblasts of the renal cortex & outer medulla in response to hypoxia (via HIF-2α transcription factor).
    • In CKD, progressive loss of functioning nephrons & chronic inflammation (TNF-α, IL-1, IFN-γ) suppress HIF-2α activity → EPO production falls despite renal hypoxia (the "relative EPO deficiency" — anaemic CKD patients have inappropriately normal/low EPO levels).
    • Result: marrow stimulation inadequate for the degree of anaemia.
  2. Uraemic inhibitors of erythropoiesis
    • Uraemic toxins (polyamines — spermine, spermidine; parathyroid hormone; "middle molecules") directly suppress erythroid colony-forming units (CFU-E & BFU-E) in bone marrow and reduce erythroblast proliferation.
    • Secondary hyperparathyroidism causes marrow fibrosis (osteitis fibrosa cystica) — "myelofibrosis of uraemia".
  3. Reduced red cell survival (haemolysis)
    • Uraemic membrane damage & oxidative stress reduce RBC deformability and lifespan (from 120 → ~70–80 days).
    • Mild extravascular haemolysis; echinocytes (burr cells) on smear.
    • Severe secondary hyperparathyroidism → microangiopathic haemolysis.
  4. Blood loss
    • Uraemic platelet dysfunction (acquired von Willebrand defect, abnormal TXA2 release) → chronic GI blood loss, blood retention in dialyser, frequent blood sampling.
    • Iron deficiency develops (absolute or functional — reticuloendothelial block from hepcidin).
  5. Iron metabolism & hepcidin
    • Inflammation & reduced renal clearance raise hepcidin → ferroportin internalisation → iron trapped in macrophages & enterocytes → functional iron deficiency (high ferritin, low TSAT).
    • ESAs (erythropoiesis-stimulating agents) increase iron demand, unmasking iron deficiency.
  6. Folate / B12 deficiency — dialysis removes folate; dietary restriction and GI losses contribute.
  7. Aluminium toxicity (historical — from aluminium-containing phosphate binders & dialysis water) → microcytic anaemia resistant to iron and EPO.
  8. ACE inhibitors / ARBs — accumulate N-acetyl-seryl-aspartyl-lysyl-proline (Ac-SDKP), inhibiting erythropoiesis.

Investigation & Management

  • Hb <11 g/dL (men), <10 g/dL (women) — investigate; check ferritin, TSAT, B12, folate, reticulocytes, KFTs, PTH.
  • Treat — iron (IV preferred in HD), ESAs (epoetin alfa/beta, darbepoetin alfa, methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoetin beta) targeting Hb 10–11.5 g/dL; correct hyperparathyroidism; folate/B12 supplementation; adequate dialysis.
  • Avoid over-correction (Hb >13) — ↑ thrombosis, hypertension, CV events, tumour progression in cancer patients.

Clinical Pearl

EPO deficiency is the relative, not absolute, kind — a non-uraemic anaemic patient raises EPO 100–1000-fold; a CKD patient with the same Hb raises it only 2-fold. This explains why exogenous ESAs work dramatically. However, the 2011 TREAT trial (darbepoetin in diabetic CKD) showed that targeting normal Hb increases stroke and cardiovascular events without improving quality of life — hence current KDIGO guidance to use the lowest ESA dose achieving Hb 10–11.5 g/dL, and to consider HIF-PH inhibitors (roxadustat, daprodustat) which mimic high-altitude physiology by stabilising HIF and stimulate endogenous EPO while also improving iron metabolism.

What Is Haptoglobin?

Haptoglobin is an α2-globulin synthesised by the liver that binds free haemoglobin (Hb) in plasma with very high affinity (Kd ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ M) — forming a Hb-haptoglobin complex that is too large to be filtered by the glomerulus. This is the body's mechanism to conserve iron and prevent haemoglobin-driven renal injury & oxidative damage.

Why It Decreases in Haemolytic Anaemia

  1. Haemolysis releases free Hb — intravascular haemolysis (e.g., PNH, mismatched transfusion, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, severe immune haemolysis, malaria, clostridial sepsis) releases haemoglobin from lysed RBCs into plasma. The free Hb immediately binds haptoglobin — this complex is removed within minutes by hepatocytes (CD163 receptor-mediated endocytosis) and macrophages. As the haptoglobin-Hb complex is cleared, serum haptoglobin is consumed faster than the liver can replace it → levels fall.
  2. Haptoglobin consumption is a marker of intravascular haemolysis — normal haptoglobin levels are 30–200 mg/dL; values <30 mg/dL (or undetectable) indicate significant intravascular haemolysis. Haptoglobin is therefore an acute-phase reactant that falls in haemolysis — a paradox because most acute-phase proteins rise in inflammation.
  3. Also reduced in extravascular haemolysis, but less prominently — extravascular haemolysis (spleen/liver macrophages) does not release much free Hb into plasma; only ~10% spills over. Thus haptoglobin is most useful for intravascular haemolysis (where it is markedly low).

Complementary Markers of Intravascular Haemolysis

  • ↑ Free plasma Hb (>1 g/dL visible — "pink/golden" plasma).
  • ↓ Haptoglobin (earliest, most sensitive).
  • ↑ LDH (especially LDH-1, from RBC cytoplasm).
  • ↑ Methaemalbumin (Schumm test positive — albumin-bound haem after haem oxidation).
  • ↑ Haemopexin (binds free haeme — falls after haptoglobin is exhausted).
  • Haemosiderinuria — chronic intravascular haemolysis (e.g., PNH) → tubular cells reabsorb filtered Hb → slough into urine as haemosiderin-laden cells (Prussian blue positive).
  • ↑ Indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin — heme catabolised by macrophages.

Pitfalls

  • Haptoglobin is low in liver disease (reduced synthesis) — false positive.
  • Haptoglobin rises with inflammation, infection, malignancy, burns, steroids — a "normal" level does NOT exclude haemolysis in inflammatory states.
  • Genetic ahaptoglobinaemia (common in West African, SE Asian, Mediterranean populations — HP0 allele) → baseline undetectable without haemolysis.
  • Infants <6 months have physiological low haptoglobin.

Clinical Pearl

The haptoglobin–haemoglobin–LDH triad is the fastest bedside panel to distinguish intravascular from extravascular haemolysis: very low/absent haptoglobin + high LDH + high free Hb = intravascular; mildly reduced haptoglobin + raised LDH + indirect bilirubin = extravascular. Haptoglobin is an inverse acute-phase reactant — the only acute-phase protein that decreases in inflammation — which makes interpretation tricky in septic patients with haemolysis. The haemopexin level (also produced by liver, binds free haem not Hb) is a useful second-line marker: it falls only after haptoglobin is fully consumed, indicating severe or established intravascular haemolysis.
q0_1_3_8:
What Is a "Nutmeg Liver"?

The nutmeg liver (chronic passive congestion of the liver) is the gross appearance of the liver in chronic right-sided heart failure (or any cause of systemic venous congestion — constrictive pericarditis, tricuspid regurgitation, Budd-Chiari, pulmonary hypertension). On cut section, the liver shows a mottled red-and-yellow reticular pattern resembling the cut surface of a nutmeg seed.

Mechanism

  1. Right heart failure → systemic venous congestion — impaired right ventricular emptying raises right atrial pressure → transmitted backward into the superior & inferior vena cavae → elevated central venous pressure → congested hepatic veins & sinusoids.
  2. Centrilobular congestion — hepatic sinusoids drain into the central vein (of the hepatic lobule), which joins the hepatic vein → IVC. Raised hepatic venous pressure is transmitted backward into the central veins & centrilobular sinusoids, causing them to dilate & engorge with blood. The centrilobular zone (zone 3) — located nearest the central vein and furthest from the portal triad oxygen supply — suffers the most.
  3. Centrilobular hypoxia & necrosis — zone 3 hepatocytes are last to receive oxygenated blood from the hepatic artery. Combined congestion (raised hydrostatic pressure, low flow) and hypoxia cause centrilobular hepatocyte atrophy, fatty change, and eventually necrosis. Necrotic hepatocytes appear yellow (lipid + necrosis); congested sinusoids appear dark red. This produces the alternating red (congested sinusoids) and yellow (fatty/necrotic hepatocytes) reticular pattern = nutmeg appearance.
  4. Fibrosis (cardiac cirrhosis) — chronic congestion → centrilobular necrosis → collapse of reticulin framework & fibrosis extending outward from central veins. Bridging fibrosis between adjacent central veins (reverse lobulation) → "cardiac cirrhosis". Unlike true cirrhosis, the basic lobular architecture is preserved & regenerative nodules are absent.

Morphology

  • Gross — liver enlarged, tense capsule, rounded edges; cut surface shows mottled red (congestion) & yellow (fatty change) reticular pattern resembling nutmeg.
  • Microscopy
    • Centrilobular (zone 3) sinusoidal dilatation & congestion.
    • Hepatocyte atrophy & loss in the centrilobular region.
    • Fatty change (yellow, vacuolated hepatocytes).
    • Necrosis with neutrophil infiltrate (if acute exacerbation).
    • Central vein & sinusoidal fibrosis in long-standing cases (cardiac sclerosis/cirrhosis).
    • Portal tracts (zone 1) relatively spared.

Clinical Associations

  • Right heart failure (most common) — cor pulmonale, RV infarction, pulmonary hypertension.
  • Tricuspid regurgitation — pulsatile liver + nutmeg pattern.
  • Constrictive pericarditis / restrictive cardiomyopathy — biventricular congestion.
  • Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein thrombosis) — also causes centrilobular congestion but peripheral (zone 1) necrosis if acute.

Clinical Pearl

The nutmeg liver illustrates the lobular zonal pathology of hepatic oxygen gradients: zone 1 (periportal) gets the most oxygenated blood and is most resistant to hypoxia; zone 3 (centrilobular) is most vulnerable — to ischaemia (shock liver, CCF), toxic injury (paracetamol, CCl4, alcohol), and congestion. Chronic passive congestion rarely causes severe hepatic dysfunction because the synthetic function (zone 1) is preserved; bilirubin & INR may be mildly elevated but hepatic failure is rare. Clinically, look for tender hepatomegaly, elevated JVP, peripheral oedema, ascites, and a reversal of the normal albumin gradient — the "cardiac liver".
q0_1_3_9:
Concept

Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP) is an autoimmune destruction of platelets (IgG antibodies against platelet membrane glycoproteins IIb/IIIa and/or Ib/IX) by splenic macrophages → isolated thrombocytopenia with normal coagulation factors.

Bleeding Time (BT) — Tests Primary Haemostasis (Platelet Plug)

  • BT (Ivy or Duke method) measures the time to haemostasis after a standard skin incision — evaluates vascular response + platelet adhesion/aggregation/activation.
  • Requires adequate platelet count (>100 × 10⁹/L) and function.
  • In ITP, platelets are destroyed by autoantibodies → count falls (typically <50 × 10⁹/L, severe bleeding <20 × 10⁹/L).
  • Even though the remaining platelets are young & functionally hyperactive (large "stress platelets"), the absolute number is insufficient to form a primary plug → BT is prolonged (typically >9 min, may exceed 15 min).
  • Other primary haemostasis tests prolonged: PFA-100 closure time (modern replacement for BT), platelet count.

PT and aPTT — Tests Secondary Haemostasis (Coagulation Cascade)

  • PT measures the extrinsic + common pathway (Factors VII, X, V, II, I). Used to monitor warfarin; sensitive to factor VII (shortest half-life).
  • aPTT measures the intrinsic + common pathway (Factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II, I, prekallikrein, HMWK). Used to monitor heparin; sensitive to factor VIII & IX.
  • Both tests require platelet-poor plasma and add phospholipid substitute + activator; platelet number is irrelevant.
  • Since ITP only destroys platelets and does NOT affect coagulation factor synthesis or function, the coagulation cascade proceeds normally → PT & aPTT remain normal.

Lab Profile of ITP

TestITP ResultRationale
Platelet count↓ DecreasedAutoantibody-mediated destruction
Bleeding time / PFA-100↑ ProlongedInsufficient platelets for primary plug
PTNormalCoagulation factors unaffected
aPTTNormalCoagulation factors unaffected
Peripheral smearThrombocytopenia; large plateletsYoung, stress platelets from compensatory marrow
Bone marrow↑ MegakaryocytesCompensatory production
Anti-platelet antibodiesPositive (IIb/IIIa)Autoimmune

Clinical Pearl

The dissociation between prolonged BT (platelet function/number) and normal PT/aPTT (coagulation factors) is the laboratory signature of any pure platelet disorder — ITP, TTP, HUS, DIC (early), qualitative platelet defects (Glanzmann, Bernard-Soulier), or von Willebrand disease (where BT prolongs but aPTT may also prolong). Conversely, in haemophilia, BT is normal but aPTT is prolonged. This dissociation teaches the central concept of haemostasis: primary haemostasis (platelet plug) is functionally independent of secondary haemostasis (fibrin cascade) — they can fail separately. Modern practice has largely replaced the BT with the PFA-100 closure time, which is more reproducible and uses collagen/ADP or collagen/epinephrine cartridges to test platelet function under shear.

What Is a Hydatidiform Mole?

A hydatidiform mole (molar pregnancy) is an abnormal conception characterised by abnormal trophoblastic proliferation and vesicular swelling of chorionic villi. It is a subset of gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD) and is classified into complete (70–80%) and partial moles.

Why β-hCG Is Markedly Elevated

  1. Trophoblastic hyperproliferation — β-hCG is synthesised by the syncytiotrophoblast (the outer multinucleated layer of the chorionic villus). In molar pregnancy, there is diffuse trophoblastic hyperplasia (both cytotrophoblast & syncytiotrophoblast), so the β-hCG-secreting cell mass is far greater than in a normal pregnancy. In a complete mole, the entire chorionic villous trophoblast proliferates diffusely; in a partial mole, focal proliferation occurs.
  2. Absence of normal fetal tissue — in a complete mole (46,XX or 46,XY, androgenetic, no maternal DNA), there is no fetus. All trophoblastic energy is devoted to proliferation & hCG production; there is no fetal metabolism or downregulation.
  3. Large villous surface area — molar villi swell into grape-like vesicles (1–2 cm), greatly increasing the surface area of trophoblastic tissue relative to a normal early pregnancy.
  4. β-subunit — β-hCG (the beta subunit specific to hCG) is measured because it does not cross-react with LH, FSH, TSH. The total β-hCG produced is proportional to the total mass of proliferating trophoblast.

Typical β-hCG Levels

  • Normal pregnancy at 8–10 weeks: 50,000–100,000 mIU/mL (peak).
  • Complete mole: typically >100,000 mIU/mL, often >1,000,000 mIU/mL — ~10–100× higher than gestational age-matched normal pregnancy.
  • Partial mole: lower (may be within normal range or moderately elevated); diagnosis often made histologically.

Other Features of Molar Pregnancy

  • Complete — 46,XX/XY androgenetic (empty ovum fertilised by one or two sperm); no fetus; diffuse villous oedema & trophoblastic hyperplasia; uterine size > dates; vaginal bleeding (prune-juice); passage of grape-like vesicles; hyperemesis; early pre-eclampsia (<20 wk); hyperthyroidism (hCG acts on TSH receptor); bilateral theca-lutein cysts (hCG-driven ovarian hyperstimulation); 15–20% risk of persistent GTN / choriocarcinoma.
  • Partial — triploid (69,XXY or XXX/XYY); fetus present but malformed; focal hydropic villi; focal trophoblastic hyperplasia; mild hCG elevation; <5% risk of invasive mole/choriocarcinoma.

Clinical Pearl

The classical triad — vaginal bleeding, uterine size larger than dates, and passing grape-like vesicles — with β-hCG >100,000 mIU/mL & the characteristic "snowstorm" / "cluster of grapes" ultrasound appearance (no fetus, no amniotic fluid, multiple hypoechoic areas) makes the diagnosis. Hyperthyroidism occurs because β-hCG shares the same α-subunit with TSH, LH, FSH and can activate the TSH receptor at high concentrations — resolving after uterine evacuation. Histopathology is mandatory to distinguish complete, partial, and invasive moles and to look for choriocarcinoma. Post-evacuation, weekly β-hCG must be followed until undetectable for 3 weeks, then monthly for 6 months — persistent elevation or rise indicates persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN) requiring methotrexate chemotherapy. Pregnancy must be avoided during follow-up (hCG from a new pregnancy would mask recurrence).

Clinical Identification

The 45-year-old man with sudden severe pain and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint after a heavy feast is the classic presentation of acute gouty arthritis (podagra). The triggering meal (purine-rich: red meat, organ meat, seafood, alcohol — especially beer) raises serum urate acutely, precipitating crystals in the joint.

Mechanism of Joint Injury in Acute Gout

  1. Hyperuricaemia & crystal formation — uric acid is the end product of purine metabolism (xanthine oxidase converts hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid). When serum urate exceeds its solubility limit (>6.8 mg/dL, especially >9 mg/dL), it precipitates as monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in joints, soft tissues, and kidneys. Cooler peripheral joints (great toe, ankle, knee) and traumatised tissues are favoured sites.
  2. Crystal shedding into joint space — a heavy meal or alcohol binge acutely raises urate levels, altering the solubility equilibrium. Pre-existing deposits (tophi) shed crystals into the synovial fluid, where they are recognised as "danger signals".
  3. Innate immune activation via NLRP3 inflammasome — MSU crystals are phagocytosed by macrophages & neutrophils; they activate the NLRP3 (NALP3) inflammasome → caspase-1 activation → cleavage of pro-IL-1β & pro-IL-18 into active forms → massive release of IL-1β (the key cytokine). IL-1β activates endothelium → recruits neutrophils via TNF-α, IL-6, IL-8, CXCL1.
  4. Neutrophil influx & inflammation — neutrophils phagocytose crystals but cannot digest them (uricase was lost in humans during evolution); crystal-induced lysosomal rupture releases proteases, ROS, leukotrienes (LTB4), and prostaglandins → acute synovitis with heat, redness, swelling, & exquisite pain.
  5. Recurrent attacks → chronic tophaceous gout — persistent hyperuricaemia forms tophi (white, chalky nodules of urate crystals surrounded by macrophages, multinucleated giant cells, fibrosis) in joints, pinnae, Achilles tendon, olecranon bursa → cartilage & bone erosion, deformity.

Crystal Appearance under Polarised Microscopy

  • Monosodium urate (gout) — needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. When the red compensator filter is used, crystals parallel to the axis appear yellow, perpendicular appear blue. Located intracellularly in neutrophils during acute attack; also extracellular.
  • Contrast with calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD — pseudogout): rhomboid-shaped, weakly positive birefringent; found in knee, wrist; affects older adults.

Pathophysiology of Hyperuricaemia

  • Overproduction (10%) — myelo-/lymphoproliferative disorders, tumour lysis syndrome, psoriasis, high-purine diet, alcohol, fructose, inherited (HPRT deficiency — Lesch-Nyhan, PRPP synthetase overactivity).
  • Underexcretion (90%) — CKD, thiazides/loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin, cyclosporine, lead nephropathy, alcohol, metabolic syndrome, hyperparathyroidism.

Clinical Pearl

The first MTP joint (podagra) is involved in >50% of first attacks because it is the coolest, most distal joint and bears the most mechanical stress. Acute management: NSAIDs (indomethacin), colchicine (microtubule inhibitor blocking NLRP3 inflammasome & neutrophil migration), or glucocorticoids — never start allopurinol during an acute attack (it worsens the attack by mobilising stores). Colchicine is most effective if given within 12 hours of onset. Long-term urate-lowering (febuxostat, allopurinol — xanthine oxidase inhibitors; probenecid — uricosuric) is started 2 weeks after the attack resolves, targeting serum urate <6 mg/dL (or <5 in tophaceous gout). Newer agents: anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist), canakinumab (anti-IL-1β monoclonal) for refractory acute gout — directly targeting the inflammasome pathway.
